(p-4503) Then Allah, exalted is He, explained what He permitted regarding not seeking permission, with His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 24, verse 29:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[29] ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering﴾, i.e., without seeking permission. ﴿Houses not inhabited﴾, i.e., not prepared for the habitation of a particular group, but for benefiting from them by whoever may be [there], such as inns (khanat), bathhouses (hammamat), and guesthouses (buyut al-diyafat). ﴿In which there is provision for you﴾, i.e., benefit and need. ﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ is a warning to whoever enters any of these places for corruption or for looking into private areas (awrat). Related from Abu al-Su'ud.

Then, glorified is He, guided to great etiquettes that encompass those who seek permission upon entering and others, by His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do.﴾

﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾: that is, the requirement of your faith is to lower the gaze from what Allah, exalted is He, has forbidden looking at. ﴿And guard their private parts﴾: that is, from exposing them to what is forbidden, or from displaying and uncovering them. ﴿That﴾: that is, the lowering and the guarding. ﴿Is purer for them﴾: that is, more purifying for the soul and more protective of the religion. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do﴾: that is, of their deeds and their conditions. He knows how they turn their eyes and how they use all their senses and limbs. So they, having known this, must be mindful and wary of it in every movement and stillness. This is what al-Zamakhshari conveyed.

Remarks:

The first: al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): The verse prohibits looking at women and at the private parts of men, and prohibits uncovering them. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah: Everything in the Qur'an that mentions "guarding the private parts" refers to fornication, except this verse and the one that follows it, which means that a man should not look at another man's private parts, nor a woman at another woman's private parts. End of quote.

This is not a necessary restriction. In that case, the prohibition of fornication is understood from it by way of a stronger implication (al-awla). Or, guarding from exposure implies guarding from exposing it to what is forbidden.

The second: If it is asked: Why did He use "min" (the partitive min, indicating a part) with lowering the gaze, and restrict it with it, but not with guarding the private parts? Even though guarding the private parts is not unrestricted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5-6]. The answer is that what is excepted from guarding is spouses and concubines, and this is few in comparison to everything else, so it is treated as if it were nonexistent and was not restricted by it, even though it is known from the other verse. This differs from the gaze, which is used unrestrictedly and is permitted in most things, except looking at what is forbidden deliberately. So the lowering was restricted by it. The object of the partitive "min" should be less than the remainder. It was also said: The lowering and the guarding are both from strangers. Some lowering of the gaze is forbidden with respect to them, and some of it is permitted, unlike guarding, so there is no reason for "min" to enter into it. Thus it is in (al-Inaya).

The third: The wisdom of placing the lowering of the gaze before the guarding of the private parts is that the gaze is the messenger of fornication and the scout of immorality, as the poet al-Hamasi said:

"When you sent your glance as a scout for your heart one day, the sights wore you out."

And because the trial in it is greater and more frequent, and one can hardly guard oneself against it. So it was hastened to prevent it. And because it actually precedes immorality, so the arrangement of the text was made in accordance with that.

The fourth: Lowering the gaze is a remedy for treating the diseases of the hearts. It cuts off their source before they arise, for a glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis. Whoever lets loose his glances, his regrets will last.

"Every calamity begins from a look, and most of a great fire comes from a small spark."

The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said in (al-Jawab al-Shafi): In lowering the gaze there are several benefits:

One: Obeying the command of Allah is the ultimate happiness of the servant in his life and his afterlife. The servant has nothing more beneficial in this world and the next than obeying the commands of his Lord, blessed and exalted is He. No one has been made happy in this world and the next except by obeying the commands of his Lord, and no one has been made wretched in this world and the next except by neglecting His commands.

Two: It prevents the effect of the poisoned arrow, which may be his destruction, from reaching his heart.

Three: It bequeaths to the heart intimacy with Allah and attentiveness toward Allah, for letting loose the gaze scatters and disperses the heart and distances it from Allah. There is nothing more harmful to the servant than letting loose the gaze, for it creates estrangement between the servant and his Lord.

Four: It strengthens the heart and gladdens it, just as letting loose the gaze weakens it and saddens it.

Five: It gives the heart light, just as letting loose the gaze gives it darkness. For this reason He, glorified is He, mentioned the verse of light right after the command to lower the gaze. He said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, then He said immediately after that: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35], meaning: the likeness of His light in the heart of His believing servant, who obeyed His commands and avoided His prohibitions. When the heart is illuminated, the delegations of goodness come to it from every side, just as when it is darkened, the clouds of trial and evil come upon it from every place. Whatever innovation and misguidance, following of desire and avoiding of guidance, turning away from the causes of happiness, and occupation with the causes of wretchedness you wish, this is only revealed to him by the light that is in the heart. When that light is lost, its owner remains like a blind man who gropes in the darkness of the night.

Six: It bequeaths true insight by which one distinguishes between the righteous and the wrongdoer, and the truthful and the liar. Shah ibn Shuja' al-Kirmani used to say: Whoever adorns his outward self by following the Sunnah, and his inward self by constant vigilance, lowers his gaze from what is forbidden, restrains his soul from desires, and accustoms himself to eating what is lawful, his insight will never fail him.

This Shuja' never had insight that failed him. Allah, glorified is He, rewards the servant for his deed with something of the same kind as his deed. Whoever leaves something for Allah, Allah replaces it with something better. So when he lowers his gaze from Allah's prohibitions, Allah compensates him by letting his inner sight loose in return for restraining his gaze for Allah's sake. He opens for him the door of knowledge, faith, and gnosis, and the true, correct insight, which is only attained through the insight of the heart. The opposite of this is the blindness (al-ama) that Allah described the people of Lot with, which is the opposite of insight. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾ [al-Hijr: 72]. He described them with intoxication, which is the corruption of the intellect, and blindness, which is the corruption of insight. So attachment to forms corrupts the intellect, and blindness of insight intoxicates the heart, as the poet said:

"Intoxicated: one with the intoxication of desire, and one with the intoxication of wine. When will the one intoxicated with it awaken?"

And another said:

"They said: You have gone mad over the one you love. I said to them: Passion is greater than what afflicts madmen.
Passion, its companion never recovers for all time, and the madman is only struck down at a moment."

Seven: It bequeaths to the heart steadfastness, courage, and strength. Allah combines for him the authority of insight and proof, and the authority of power and strength, as in the report: "The one who opposes his desire, Satan flees from his shadow." The opposite of this you find in one who follows his desire: the humiliation, lowliness, disgrace, baseness, and contemptibility of the soul, and what Allah places upon those who disobey Him. As al-Hasan said: Even though they are carried by mules and ambled upon by horses, sin does not leave their necks. Allah refuses except to humiliate whoever disobeys Him. Allah, glorified is He, has made honor the companion of obedience and humiliation the companion of disobedience. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. And He said: ﴿Do not weaken and do not grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139]. Faith is speech and action, outward and inward. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever desires honor, then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous action raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10]. That is, whoever desires honor, let him seek it through obedience to Allah and His remembrance, through the good word and righteous knowledge. In the supplication of the qunut: "Indeed, one whom You have befriended is not humiliated, and one whom You have opposed is not honored." Whoever obeys Allah has befriended Him in what he obeyed Him in, and has honor according to the measure of his obedience. Whoever disobeys Him has opposed Him in what he disobeyed Him in, and has humiliation according to the measure of his disobedience.

Eight: It closes off the entry of Satan into the heart. For he enters with the glance and penetrates to the heart along with it, faster than desire penetrates an empty place. He then presents to him the image of the one looked at, adorns it, and makes it an idol to which the heart devotes itself. Then he promises and deceives him. He kindles the fire of lust in the heart and throws upon it the firewood of sins, which he could not have reached without that image. So the heart becomes within the flame. From that flame come those breaths in which one finds the heat of fire, and those sighs and burnings. The heart is surrounded by fires from every side. It is in their midst like a sheep in the midst of an oven. For this reason the punishment of the people of desires through forbidden images is that a fiery oven is prepared for them in the barzakh, and their spirits are deposited in it until their bodies are resurrected, as Allah showed His Prophet ﷺ in a dream, in the hadith agreed upon as authentic.

Nine: It empties the heart for thinking about its interests and occupation with them. Letting loose the gaze scatters this and comes between him and them. So his affairs fall into disorder, and he falls into following his desire and into heedlessness of his Lord's command. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair has become excess﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. Letting loose the gaze necessitates these three matters in proportion to it.

Ten: Between the eye and the heart there is a passage and a path that causes each of them to be affected by the other, and each is set right by the other's rectitude and corrupted by the other's corruption. When the heart is corrupted, the gaze is corrupted, and when the gaze is corrupted, the heart is corrupted. The same is true on the side of righteousness. When the eye is ruined and corrupted, the heart is ruined and corrupted, and becomes like a garbage heap, which is the place of impurities, filth, and dirt. It is not fit to be the abode of knowledge of Allah, love of Him, turning to Him, intimacy with Him, and joy in His nearness. Only the opposites of these dwell in it. This is an indication of some of the benefits of lowering the gaze, which will reveal to you what lies beyond them. End of quote.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded the women with what He commanded the men, and added to their command what He obligated of abandoning the jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) customs that were familiar to them before, by His saying, glorified is He:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[31] ﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze, guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what appears of it, and to draw their head-coverings (khumur) over their chests (juyub), and not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or their husbands' fathers, or their sons, or their husbands' sons, or their brothers, or their brothers' sons, or their sisters' sons, or their women, or those whom their right hands possess, or male attendants who have no desire (for women), or children who have not yet become aware of women's private matters. And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment becomes known. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you may be successful.﴾

﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾, that is: by covering themselves and guarding themselves against fornication, as has already been explained. Al-Zamakhshari said: Women too are commanded to lower their gaze. It is not permissible for a woman to look at a non-mahram man at anything from beneath his navel to his knee. If she desires (to look), she should lower her gaze entirely. She should not look at a woman except at the same (parts). Lowering her gaze from non-mahrams altogether is more fitting and better for her. From this is the hadith of Ibn Umm Maktum, from Umm Salama (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ), and Maymuna was with him. Ibn Umm Maktum came, and that was after we had been commanded to observe hijab. He entered upon us, and he (ﷺ) said: 'Veil yourselves.' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Is he not blind, unable to see us?' He said: 'Are you two blind? Do you not see him?'" This hadith was related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, and he (al-Tirmidhi) authenticated it.

﴿And not display their adornment except what appears of it﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: Adornment (zina) is that with which a woman adorns herself, of jewelry, kohl, or dye. What is apparent of it, such as the ring, the fatkha (a large ring), kohl, and dye, there is no harm in displaying to non-mahrams. What is hidden of it, such as the bracelet, the anklet, the armlet, the necklace, the crown, the sash, and the earring, she should not display except to those mentioned. He mentioned the adornment rather than its places, for emphasis on the command to guard and cover oneself, because these adornments are attached to parts of the body which it is not permissible to look at for anyone other than these (persons). These are the forearm, the shin, the upper arm, the neck, the head, the chest, and the ear. He forbade displaying the adornments themselves, so that it would be known that if looking was not permitted to her because of her contact with those places, then, by evidence that looking at her when she is not in contact with them is beyond dispute as to its permissibility, looking at the very places themselves is firmly prohibited and is established as unlawful, bearing witness that women have the duty to be careful in covering them and to fear Allah in regard to uncovering them.

(Question): Why was the apparent adornment permitted without restriction? I say: Because covering it entails hardship. A woman cannot avoid handling things with her hands, and from the need to uncover her face, especially in testimony, litigation, and marriage. She is also obliged to walk in the streets and her feet become visible, especially poor women. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿except what appears of it﴾, meaning: except what customary practice and natural disposition have made apparent, and the basis in this is apparency. End.

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Ikleel): Ibn 'Abbas interpreted His words ﴿except what appears of it﴾ as the face and the two palms, as Ibn Abi Hatim related. Those who permit looking at a woman's face and palms, where there is no temptation, rely on this; and whoever says that her private part is what lies beyond these two (says otherwise). Ibn Mas'ud interpreted it as clothing, and interpreted adornment as the ring, the bracelet, the earring, the necklace, and the anklet. Ibn Abi Hatim also related this. So it is evidence for one who does not permit looking at any part of her body and considers all of it to be private part.

﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾, that is: let them cover themselves with their veils (maqani'), their hair, their necks, their earrings, and their chests, by casting them over their juyub, that is, their places, which are the throat and the chest.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Their juyub were wide, so their throats and chests and what surrounds them would show. They used to let the khumur hang down behind them, leaving (the front) uncovered, so they were commanded to let them hang down in front until they cover them. It is permissible that by juyub is meant the chests, by naming what is adjacent to and in contact with them, and from this is the saying: "Naasih al-jayb" (a proverb).

A subtle point: Abu Hayyan said: "yadribna" is transitive with "'ala" because it implies the meaning of placing. Al-Raghib made it (transitive) with it without implication. And "al-khumur" is the plural of khimar, which in linguistic usage refers to what is used to cover. Custom restricted it to what a woman covers her head with. From it come the verbs "ikhtamarat" and "takhammarat" (she covered her head). And "al-jayb" is what is cut (jiba), that is, cut from the top of a shirt, which the common people call a collar (tawq). As for applying it to what is at the side for placing dirhams and the like, this is not from Arabic speech, as Ibn Taymiyya mentioned. Thus (it is stated) in (al-'Inaya).

Then He repeated the prohibition on displaying adornment, to make an exception for some of the permitted categories from it, in terms of the one who looks, after having made an exception from it of some categories of necessity in terms of the one looked at, by His words: ﴿and not display their adornment except to their husbands﴾, that is, for they are the ones intended by the adornment. They are permitted to look at all of her body, even the private part, but with disapproval according to the well-known view.

Imam Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Qattan said in the book (Ihkam al-Nazar): From Asbagh: "There is no harm in it, and it is not disliked." It is related from Malik: "There is no harm in looking at the private part during intercourse." Then we mention that what is related, that this causes blindness, is a hadith that is not authentic, because in its chain is Baqiyya, and they have said: "Most of Baqiyya's hadiths are not pure." And it has not been transmitted from the Arabs that this is disliked. Al-Nabigha, al-A'sha, Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Mayyada, 'Abd Bani al-Hassas, and al-Farazdaq have well-known verses on this matter.

And His words: ﴿or their fathers, or their husbands' fathers, or their sons, or their husbands' sons, or their brothers, or their brothers' sons, or their sisters' sons﴾, that is: because these are their mahrams, from whom temptation is safe. Their fathers are their guardians who protect them from what harms them. The fathers of their husbands protect their sons from what would harm them. Their sons, by nature, serve their mothers, and they are of them. The sons of their husbands, by nature, serve their fathers and the beloved ones of their fathers. Their brothers are the guardians after the fathers, and their sons are guardians after them. Likewise the sons of their sisters are, in kinship, like the sons of their brothers, so they are shamed by the attribution of evil to the maternal aunt, just as they would be shamed by its attribution to the paternal aunt. This is what al-Mahayimi indicated.

Al-Zamakhshari summarized this by saying: The hidden adornment was permitted to those mentioned, because they are specifically the ones with whom there is a pressing need to interact and associate, and because temptation is unlikely to come from them, and because of the natural aversion in human dispositions to intimacy with close relatives. A woman needs their company on journeys, for alighting, mounting, and other matters.

And His words: ﴿or their women﴾. It was said: they are believing women, taking this from the possessive form. So it is not permissible for a believing woman to strip before a polytheist or a People of the Book woman. It was also said: all women, for they are equal in permissibility of looking at one another.

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Ikleel): In this is the permissibility of a woman's looking at a woman as a mahram would. Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ata': When the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Bayt al-Maqdis, their midwives were Jewish and Christian women.

Al-Razi said: The second view is the doctrine, and the view of the early predecessors is understood as recommendation and preference.

And His words: ﴿or those whom their right hands possess﴾, that is: because of their need for them. If their entry upon them were forbidden, they would be compelled. Thus said al-Mahayimi. The apparent meaning of the verse includes male slaves and female slaves, and a group went to this view. They said: there is no harm for them in displaying to their slaves of their adornment what they display to their mahrams. They also argued with what Abu Dawud related from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to Fatima with a slave whom he had given her as a gift. He said: And upon Fatima was a garment, which, if she covered her head with it, did not reach her feet, and if she covered her feet with it, did not reach her head. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw what she was facing, he said: 'There is no harm upon you. He is only your father and your slave.'"

It is mentioned in (Tarikh Ibn 'Asakir) that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ada was very black, with extremely dark complexion. The Prophet (may the blessings of Allah be upon him) had given him to his daughter Fatima. She raised him, then freed him, and then he was afterward with Mu'awiya against 'Ali. Ibn Kathir related this, so it is possible that he is the same person. And Allah knows best.

Some people went to the view that this refers to polytheist female slaves, and that it is permissible for her to display her adornment to them even if they are polytheists. They said: The secret of singling out the female slaves, despite its being included in His words ﴿or their women﴾, is to inform that what is meant is whoever is in their company among the free women and the slaves, because the possessive in "their women" applies to free women. Like His words: ﴿two witnesses from among your men﴾ [al-Baqara: 282]. So they are joined to them in order to share in the permissibility of looking at them. But the first view is stronger, because the principle is to act upon the general unless there is evidence restricting it, especially since the wisdom in it is evident, which is the removal of hardship. This is what al-Shafi'i and the majority of his companions decided upon.

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Ikleel): On the first view, it is argued from the attribution of "right hands" that it is not permissible for the husband's slave to look. And whoever permits it argues with the reading: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa: 3].

And His words: ﴿or male attendants (al-tabi'in)﴾, that is, the servants, because they are in the sense of slaves: ﴿who have no desire (ghayr uli al-ir'a)﴾, that is, who have no need for women: ﴿of men﴾, such as the decrepit old man and the imbecile. Whoever permits the looking of a eunuch relies on this. And His words: ﴿or children who have not yet become aware of women's private matters (awrat)﴾, that is, they do not understand their conditions because of their youth. So it is used as evidence for the prohibition of looking by an adolescent who understands these matters, just like an adult, as in (al-Ikleel).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (yazharu) is either from "zahara 'ala al-shay'" when one becomes aware of something, meaning they do not know what is a private part and do not distinguish between it and other things; or from "zahara 'ala fulan" when one prevails over him, and "zahara 'ala al-Qur'an" meaning he memorized it and was able to do so; that is, they have not reached the age of capacity for sexual intercourse. And "al-tifl" is singular but used in place of the plural, as indicated by its being described with a plural, and similar to it is "al-hajj" meaning "al-hajjaj" (pilgrims). Al-Raghib said that it applies to the plural.

A reminder: Al-Suyuti said in (al-Ikleel): Some have argued from His words: ﴿and not display their adornment except﴾, etc., that looking is not permitted for the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle, because they are not mentioned in the verse. Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrima, who said: He did not mention the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle because they describe women to their sons, and she does not remove her head-covering in front of the paternal uncle or the maternal uncle.

Al-Razi said: The apparent view is that they are, like the rest of the mahrams, permitted to look. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. He said: Because the verse does not mention foster-nursing, which is like lineage. And he said in Surah al-Ahzab: ﴿there is no blame upon them concerning their fathers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 55], the verse, and did not mention in it husbands or their sons. Yet they are mentioned here. And sometimes a part is mentioned to draw attention to the whole.

Then he said: In al-Sha'bi's statement there are eloquent indications of the obligation upon them to be extremely careful in covering themselves.

(p-4515) Then He, exalted is He, pointed out that adornment, just as it must be concealed from sight, must also be concealed from hearing if it has an effect on desire, by His words, glorified is He:

﴿And let them not stamp their feet﴾, that is, on the ground: ﴿so that what they conceal﴾, that is, from sight: ﴿of their adornment becomes known﴾, such as the anklet. This is a prohibition of what some of them used to do, namely striking their feet on the ground so that their anklets would jingle and it would be known that they were adorned with it. For that stirs up men's desire for them and creates the impression that they have a desire for men.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "When they are forbidden to make the sound of their jewelry heard after being forbidden to display the jewelry itself, it is known from this that the prohibition against displaying the places of the jewelry is more and more emphatic." It was said: "And when it is forbidden to listen to the sound of their jewelry, then listening to their voices is all the more forbidden." This is a blocking of the paths to what is forbidden (*sadd li-bab al-muharramat*, the closing of the gateways to prohibited things), and an instruction in the more cautious course, especially in places of suspicion and in what may serve as a means (*dhari'a*, a pretext or pathway) to them.

Notice (*tanbih*):

Ibn Kathir said: This prohibition includes everything of her adornment that was concealed, when she moves in a way that reveals what was hidden of it. Among this is what has been reported of her being forbidden to wear perfume and scent when she leaves her house, so that men may smell her fragrance. Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Musa, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every eye commits adultery. And when a woman applies perfume and then passes by a gathering, she is such-and-such," meaning an adulteress.

He said: From the same chapter is the hadith from Abu Hurayrah. This is a hasan sahih hadith, and Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i also related it. Al-Tirmidhi also related from Maymunah bint Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The woman who flaunts her adornment among those who are not her people is like a darkness on the Day of Resurrection, having no light."

Also among this is their prohibition from walking in the middle of the road, because of the display (*tabarruj*) it involves. Abu Dawud related from Abu Usayd al-Ansari that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was coming out of the mosque, and men had mixed with women in the road. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the women: "Fall back, for it is not for you to walk in the middle of the road. Keep to the sides of the road." So the woman would press herself against the wall, until her garment would catch on the wall from her pressing against it.

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾, that is: return to Him by acting on His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, for the requirement of your faith is that. ﴿That you may succeed﴾, that is: so that you may attain the happiness of both abodes.

When the Exalted forbade fornication and its near and distant beginnings, He commanded marriage. For marriage, although it is intended in itself, as the basis for the preservation of the human species, is the best deterrent from that. So He, glorified is He, said:

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 24, verse 32:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[32] ﴿And marry off the unmarried (al-ayama) among you and your righteous male and female slaves. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿And marry off the unmarried among you and your male and female slaves﴾ means: arrange marriages for whoever has no spouse among the free men and women, and for whoever among your young male slaves and female slaves is fit for it. The address is to the guardians and the masters. "Al-ayama" is the plural of "ayyim," one who has no wife or who has no husband, whether for a man or a woman. It is said: "aama" and "aamat" and "ta'ayyama," when neither of them marries, whether they are virgins or previously married.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The consideration of righteousness applies to the slaves, because whoever among them lacks righteousness is not fit for his master to care for his affairs, to show him compassion, or to take pains in arranging his interests with what is necessary, legally and customarily, of spending wealth and benefits. Rather, his right is that the master should not keep him for himself. As for the non-consideration of righteousness (p-4517) among the free men and free women, it is because righteousness generally prevails among them, and because they have independent authority over their own affairs and their property. So when they resolve to marry, the guardians must assist them, since there is no loss incurred by them in this, such that a gain returning to them in exchange would need to be considered, whether immediate or deferred. It has also been said: the intended meaning is readiness for marriage and fulfilling its rights.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ is a removal of what might be a deterrent from marriage, arising from the poverty of one of the two parties. That is: let the poverty of the suitor or the betrothed not prevent them from marrying. For in the bounty of Allah, mighty and majestic, there is sufficiency from wealth, for He is ever bestowing and providing. He gives provision to whom He wills from where he does not reckon. Or it is a promise from Him, glorified is He, of enrichment, but it is conditional upon His will, as in His saying: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ means: He is Rich, possessing vastness, whom the enrichment of creatures does not diminish, since His blessing has no end and His power has no limit. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ — He extends provision to whom He wills and measures it as wisdom requires. End of Abu Mas'ud's words.

Remarks:

First: The command in the verse is for recommendation (nadb), because it is known that marriage is a recommended matter. It may be obligatory for the guardians when the woman requests it.

In al-Iklil: Al-Shafi'i used the command as evidence for the requirement of a guardian (wali), because the address is to him, and because a woman cannot independently contract her own marriage. Those who permit the marriage of slave women without condition, and the marriage of a slave to a free woman, have used the general wording of the verse as evidence. Those who say that a master may be compelled to marry off his male and female slaves have also used it as evidence.

Second: We have stated that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ is conditional upon His will. So it is not said that He does not break His promise, and how many a married man is poor? The restriction by His will is based on a textual proof, namely the verse mentioned earlier, or the indication of His saying: {All-Knowing, All-Wise}, because its outcome leads to the will. Or it is based on reason, namely that the Wise does only what wisdom requires.

(p-4518) Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: One may say: If His will is what is taken into account regarding the wealth of the married person, then it is also what is taken into account regarding the wealth of the unmarried person. So what is the point of linking the promise of wealth to marriage, given that the condition of the one who marries is divided in wealth according to His will, so that some are enriched by it and some are poor, just as the condition of the one who does not marry is divided?

The answer, and success is from Allah: The benefit of linking wealth to marriage is that human nature has been established in tending toward reliance on causes and depending upon them, and in heedlessness of the Causer, may He be exalted. To the point that delusion dominates the intellect, so it is imagined that a large number of dependents is a cause that necessarily produces poverty, and their absence is a cause that definitely produces the accumulation of wealth. And that neither of these two causes influences what delusion has attached to it. So it is intended to uproot this imagining that has become fixed in nature, by announcing that Allah, exalted is He, may indeed accumulate wealth and make it grow despite a large number of dependents, which in the imaginations is a cause of its depletion. And He may decree destitution despite their absence, which in the imaginations is a cause of abundance. Reality bears witness to this without dispute. This definitively shows that the causes which humans imagine are linked to their effects with an inseparable link is not as they claim. Rather, the Determiner of causes decrees wealth and poverty, and that decree is contingent upon nothing but a particular will. In that case, the intelligent and alert person does not recoil from marriage, because it has become established for him that it has no effect on poverty, and that Allah, exalted is He, is not prevented by it from enriching him. Likewise, abstaining from marriage for the sake of accumulating wealth has no effect, because it is established that it has no influence in this regard, and that no obstacle prevents Allah, exalted is He, from restricting provision for him. And if the servant takes up a cause, let him not look to it, but to the will of Allah, exalted and sanctified is He. So the meaning of His saying in that case: ﴿If they are poor﴾ to the end of the verse is that marriage does not prevent them from the wealth of Allah's bounty. Thus the negation of its being an obstacle to wealth is expressed by its existence alongside wealth. Nothing removes the obstructive quality except the existence of what is imagined as prevented together with what is imagined as preventing, even in one case among the cases, as a result of that. From this valley come examples such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. The apparent meaning of the command is a request to disperse upon the conclusion of the prayer, but that is not the literal intended meaning. Rather, the purpose is to establish the removal of the obstacle, which is the prayer, and to show that once the prayer is concluded, there is no obstacle. So the negation of the obstacle is expressed by dispersal, in a way that conveys a demand for dispersal, as an exaggeration in establishing the meaning for the listener. And Allah knows best.

Reflect upon this section and take it as a support wherever there is need for it. End.

Third: In al-Iklil: Some have used this verse as evidence that a marriage is not annulled due to inability to provide maintenance (nafaqah), because He said: "Allah will enrich them," and did not separate between them.

Then, after explaining the permissibility of marrying the poor, Allah, exalted is He, guided those unable to obtain the means of marriage to what is better for them, with His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 24, verse 33:

The discussion of the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[33] ﴿And let those who do not find a marriage (nikah) keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those among your slaves who seek a deed of manumission (kitab), write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, when they desire chastity, in order that you may seek the commodity of worldly life. And whoever compels them - indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿And let those who do not find a marriage keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ That is: let those who do not find a marriage strive to be chaste. "Marriage" (nikah) here means its causes, or the ability to marry, that is, getting married. So it is by way of metaphor, or by supposing an elided noun. Or it is intended that "nikah" means that by which one marries (i.e., the means/dowry).

Al-Shihab said: "Fi'al" may be an adjective in the sense of a passive participle, like kitab in the sense of maktub (written), and an instrument noun, like rikab for that which is ridden with. And this is common, as the lexicographers have stated. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾, is an encouragement for those who keep themselves chaste and an advance promise of superiority to them through wealth, so that the waiting for that and the hoping for it becomes a kindness to them in their chastity and a fortifying of their hearts. And so that it may become clear through this that His bounty is more fitting for the chaste and closer to the righteous. How excellent is the ordering of these commands: He first commanded what protects from temptation and keeps away from committing sin, which is lowering the gaze; then marriage, by which one protects one's religion and the independence through the lawful from the unlawful is achieved; then restraining the commanding-to-evil self and turning it away from aspiring to desire when unable to marry, until one is granted the ability to do so. This is what al-Zamakhshari stated.

Note:

In al-Iklil, it is said: The verse indicates the recommendation of patience regarding marriage for one who is unable to bear its burden. Some have used this verse to argue for the invalidity of temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah).

When the Exalted commanded masters to marry off their righteous male and female slaves, despite their servitude, He encouraged them to write a manumission agreement with them if they requested that, so that they might become free and manage their own affairs as free persons. Thus He said, exalted is He: ﴿and those who seek a deed (kitab)﴾, i.e., the writing of manumission, ﴿among those your right hands possess, write it for them﴾, out of eagerness for their emancipation, which is the original state regarding them, and out of love for realizing equality in human brotherhood. Mukatabah (the contract of manumission) is that the master says: "I have made a contract with you" (katabtuka), i.e., I have made your freedom written upon myself, for a certain sum that you pay in certain installments. The slave accepts that, and so he becomes owner of his earnings and of what is given to him. A period of grace must accompany it, because earning cannot be conceived without it. Installments are stipulated so that the period is not left empty of service and its compensation entirely. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿if you know any good in them﴾, i.e., such as trustworthiness, so that they do not pay the installments from stolen money, and the capacity to earn and righteousness, so that he does not harm anyone after manumission. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾, is a command to the masters to give some of their wealth. Included in its ruling is remitting some of the amount of the contract. And for others, by giving them from zakat, as assistance to them in their emancipation.

Note:

In al-Iklil, it is said: The verse indicates the legislation of manumission contracts (kitabah) and that it is recommended. The people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) said: it is obligatory, due to the apparent wording of the verse. And that for its recommendation or obligation there are two conditions: the slave's request for it, and knowledge of good in him. Mujahid and others explained "good" as wealth, skill, fulfilment of promises, truthfulness, and trustworthiness.

Then the Exalted forbade the compelling of slave girls into fornication, as they had been accustomed to do in the Jahiliyyah, by His statement, glorified is He: ﴿and do not compel your slave girls﴾, i.e., your female slaves, for "fata" and "fatah" are used as euphemisms for male and female slaves. In a hadith: "Let one of you say: my young man (fatay) and my young woman (fatati), and let him not say: my slave (abdi) and my female slave (amati)." His statement, exalted is He, ﴿to prostitution (al-bigha')﴾, i.e., fornication. It is said: "baghat baghyan wa bigha'an" when she committed fornication, because she went beyond what was not hers. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿when they desire chastity﴾, is not to restrict the prohibition to the case where they desire to abstain from fornication, nor to exclude other cases from its ruling; rather it is to preserve their constant custom, since they used to compel them to prostitution while they desired to abstain from it, along with the abundance of their desire which commands immorality, and their deficiency in knowing matters, which summons to good and restrains from engaging in vices. The words of Abu al-Su'ud end.

That is: then there is no conceptual restriction in the condition, and this is like the answer of some: the usual state is that compulsion occurs only when chastity is desired. Speech that comes in the manner of what is usual does not have a restrictive implication (mafhum al-khitab). Just as khul' (divorce by compensation) is permitted outside the state of discord, but since it usually occurs in a state of discord, there is no implication from His statement, ﴿and if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. And of this kind is His statement: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear that those who disbelieve will harm you﴾ [al-Nisa': 101], and shortening is not restricted to a state of fear, but He, exalted is He, applied it as the usual case. So likewise here. The words end.

Abu al-Su'ud said: In it there is, in addition, an intensification of their condition and a censure of their vices, which is evident. For whoever has even a little manliness would hardly accept the immorality of one whom his household holds of his female slaves, let alone ordering them to it or compelling them to it, especially when they desire chastity. And the choice of the word "in" (in) instead of "idha" (when), while the desire is certainly realized in the subject of the text, is to signal the obligation to cease compulsion when the desire for chastity is within the sphere of doubt and uncertainty. How much more so when it is certain to occur, as is the reality? His statement, exalted is He, ﴿in order that you may seek the commodity of worldly life﴾, is a qualifier of the compulsion, but not in the sense that it is the basis for the prohibition, rather in the sense that it is what is customary among them, just as what came before it. It was mentioned as a censure of them for what they were engaged in, namely bearing a great burden for the sake of a paltry gain. That is: do not do what you are doing of compelling them to prostitution in pursuit of fleeting enjoyment, quickly vanishing, meaning from their earnings and their children.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and whoever compels them﴾ is a resumed sentence brought to affirm the prohibition and emphasize the obligation of acting upon it, by explaining that the compelled women are freed from the punishment of the one compelled into it, in expression, and that the harm of compulsion returns to the compellers, in allusion. That is: ﴿and whoever compels them﴾ into what was mentioned of fornication, ﴿indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, i.e., toward them. As it occurs in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, and upon it is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them. And as His statement, exalted is He, ﴿after their compulsion﴾ indicates, i.e., their being compelled. Moreover, the compulsion is a verbal noun from the passive form, for placing it between the subject of "inna" and its predicate is to signal that this is the cause of forgiveness and mercy. Al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, when he recited this verse, would say: "For them, by Allah! For them, by Allah!" In specifying the two (forgiveness and mercy) for them and fixing their scope, together with the compellers also having been mentioned in the conditional clause, there is clear indication that they are wholly deprived of both, as if it were said: "Not for the compeller." And because this implication is evident, the text dispensed with a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun. Thus, permitting that the two attach to the compellers on condition of repentance, independently, or together with the women, disturbs the grandeur of the sublime composition and diminishes the matter of prohibition in a context of awe. The women's need for forgiveness, which indicates a prior sin, is either because, though they were compelled, they do not in the course of fornication fully escape some trace of yielding to what human nature dictates; or because compulsion may fall short of the degree of coercion that entirely removes choice; or to magnify the gravity of fornication and to urge the compelled women to hold firmly to abstaining from it, and to intensify the warning to the compellers, by showing that these women, were it not for forgiveness and mercy overtaking them, would be liable to punishment, despite the existence of an excuse on their behalf. So what of the one who compels them, regarding deserving punishment? The words of Abu al-Su'ud end, and he has excelled in establishing the aim, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

Note:

In al-Iklil, it is said: The verse contains the prohibition of compelling female slaves to fornication; that the one compelled is not accountable nor sinful; that compulsion to fornication is conceivable; that the wage of a prostitute is forbidden; and that it refutes those who make the hadd punishment obligatory upon the one who compels her.

Then the Exalted warned against opposing what He has forbidden, which He has made most clear, by His statement, glorified is He:

The commentary on the words of Allah the Exalted:

[34] ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that make things clear, and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that make things clear﴾ means: manifest, or explaining, for everything your needs require of you in matters of worship, transactions and conduct. Among them is what was mentioned before, the prohibition of compulsion (ikrah) in religion. Their meaning is not hidden. ﴿And an example from those who passed away before you﴾ means: a great report concerning the past nations and what befell them because of their wrongdoing and their transgression of the limits of Allah. ﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ means: they take heed by it and refrain from what is not fitting for them. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 56], meaning: a lesson by which they may take warning. The singling out of the God-fearing (muttaqun) is to urge the addressees to join their ranks, for they are the successful ones. And the words of Allah the Exalted:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 1 of 2)**

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[35] ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp within a glass, the glass as if it were a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah presents examples for the people, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, the One who illuminates them with the stars and with the lights that flow from them. This is a figurative usage (majaz), in which the effect is named by its cause, as the cause is named for what it causes. Or it means the One who manages them, from the saying of people about the outstanding leader in management, "the light of the people," because they are guided by him in affairs; this is then a figurative usage. Or it is a metaphor (isti'ara), in which "the light" is borrowed to mean "the one who illuminates," i.e., the manager, by the relation of similarity in the attainment of guidance. Or it means the Originator of them both, for light is manifest in its own essence and makes other things manifest, as al-Ghazali said. Thus it is applied to Him, exalted is He, as a figurative usage by implication (majaz mursal), in consideration of a necessary meaning of its sense.

Abu al-Su'ud said: He expressed the Illuminator by "the Light" to draw attention to the strength of the illumination and the intensity of its effect, and to signal that He, exalted is He, is manifest in His own essence, while everything other than Him is manifest through His making it manifest, just as light is luminous in itself while everything else is illuminated by it. "The light" is attributed to "the heavens and the earth" to indicate the breadth of its radiance. Or the intended meaning of the two is the entire cosmos.

﴿The likeness of His light﴾: that is, the description of His light, which is wondrous in its nature. Abu al-Su'ud said: that is, His light which flows from Him, exalted is He, upon the things illuminated by it, and it is the clear Qur'an, as what precedes it indicates by its description of His verses as sent down and clarifying. He has also explicitly stated that it is a light, in His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa: 174]. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, al-Hasan, and Zayd ibn Aslam, may Allah have mercy on them, exalted is He.

﴿as a niche﴾: that is, like the description of a recess, a window-niche, not passing through the wall, in terms of illumination and radiance. ﴿Within which is a lamp﴾: that is, a large, piercing lamp, intensely bright. It has been said: the niche (mishkah) is the tube in the middle of a lantern, and the lamp (misbah) is the blazing wick. ﴿The lamp within a glass﴾: that is, a lantern of pure, bright glass. ﴿The glass as if it were a shining star﴾: that is, glittering and blazing, resembling a pearl in its clarity and brilliance. ﴿Lit from a blessed tree﴾: that is, abundant in benefits, in that its wick is fed by its oil. ﴿An olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [p. 4525]: that is, neither an eastern one upon which the sun falls only at sunrise, nor a western one upon which it falls only at sunset, nor one that is not struck by the sun at the start of the day, but rather in a place upon which the sun shines from its first rising until its last setting, such as a desert or the top of a mountain. Therefore its oil is brightest. ﴿Whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾: that is, it would almost give light by itself without fire, because of its purity and sheen. ﴿Light upon light﴾: that is, that light by which He expressed the Qur'an, and its wondrous description has been likened to what was added to the description of the niche. It is a great light existing upon a light of the same kind. Thus "light" (nur) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the prepositional phrase is related to an omitted element as a qualifier emphasizing what the indefiniteness conveyed of grandeur. The clause is a summary of the likeness, a clarification of what resulted from it, and a preparation for what follows.

The meaning of ﴿light upon light﴾ is not one light above another of its kind, nor merely the combination of two lights, but rather it is an expression for a light that is multiplied, like the multiplication of the light of the niche through what has been mentioned. For when the lamp is in a confined place, like a niche, it is brighter for it and more gathering of its light, unlike a wide space, in which the light spreads out and disperses. The lantern is the most helpful thing for increasing illumination, and likewise the oil and its purity. Beyond these degrees there is, customarily, no further degree that increases its light in brilliance.

﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾: that is, to this piercing, great light, by enabling them to believe in it and to understand the proofs of its truth.

Abu al-Su'ud said: the manifest noun is used in place of the pronoun to increase its establishment and to affirm its intrinsic grandeur with its grandeur through attribution to His pronoun, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Allah presents examples for the people﴾: that is, so that the intelligible draws near to them from the perceptible, for clarification and explanation. For this reason He likened His light, expressed by the Qur'an, to the light of the niche.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾: that is, nothing is hidden from Him, and in this is a promise and a warning, for His knowledge is an expression for His recompense in such verses.

**Note:**
This verse, the Verse of Light, is among those verses about which special works have been composed. Among them is *Mishkat al-Anwar* (The Niche of Lights) by Imam al-Ghazali, from which al-Razi quoted a long passage in his *Tafsir* here. I have also seen, in the book of Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Juyush al-Islamiyya*, what is fitting to cite, to strengthen the point and to gain further knowledge.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Allah, glorified is He, named Himself Light, made His Book light, His Messenger (ﷺ) light, and His religion light. He veiled Himself from His creation with light, and He made the abode of His friends a shining light. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. It has been explained as meaning that He is the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth, and the Guide of the people of the heavens and the earth. By His light the people of the heavens and the earth are guided. This, however, is His action. Otherwise, the light which is one of His attributes subsists in Him, and from it is derived His name "the Light," which is one of the Most Beautiful Names. Light is attributed to Him, glorified is He, in one of two ways: the attribution of a quality to the thing it describes, and the attribution of an object to its agent. The first is like His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And the earth shines with the light of its Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 69]. This is its shining on the Day of Resurrection by His light, exalted is He, when He comes to judge. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the well-known supplication: "I seek refuge in the noble light of Your Face from being led astray; there is no god but You." In another report: "I seek refuge in Your Face—or in the light of Your Face—by which the darknesses were illuminated." So the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that the darknesses were illuminated by the light of the Face of Allah, just as He, exalted is He, informed that the earth shines on the Day of Resurrection by His light.

In *al-Mu'jam* of al-Tabarani, in his *al-Sunna*, in the book of Uthman al-Darimi, and in others, it is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "With your Lord there is no night or day; the light of the heavens and the earth is from the light of His Face." What Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said is closer to the explanation of the verse than the view of those who explained it as "the Guide of the people of the heavens and the earth." As for those who explained it as "the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth," there is no contradiction between that and the saying of Ibn Mas'ud. The truth is that He is the Light of the heavens and the earth in all these senses.

In Sahih Muslim and others, from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us and spoke five words, saying: 'Allah does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light. Were He to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn away whatever His sight reaches of His creation.'"

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'It is light; how could I see Him?'" I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, say: its meaning is that there was a light, and a light prevented seeing Him, so how could I see Him? He said: What indicates this is that in some authentic wordings: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a light." The wording of this hadith has been difficult for many people, to the point that some of them altered it, saying: "Nurani'i ara" (I see a luminous one), taking it as the relative ya', while it is one word. This is an error both in wording and in meaning. What caused this confusion and error for them is that, since they believed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord, and his saying "how could I see Him?" seemed like a denial of seeing, they became confused about the hadith, and some of them rejected it on account of the irregularity of its wording. All of this is a departure from what the evidence requires.

Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, in his book *al-Ru'ya* (The Vision), related the consensus (ijma') of the Companions that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not see his Lord on the night of the Ascension (al-Mi'raj). Some have excepted Ibn 'Abbas from those who said so. Our shaykh says: this is not really a disagreement, for Ibn 'Abbas did not say that he saw Him with his physical eyes. Ahmad, in one of his two narrations, relied on this, saying: "He (ﷺ) saw Him, mighty and majestic is He," without saying "with the eyes of his head." Ahmad's wording is the wording of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. What confirms its soundness is what our shaykh said about the meaning of the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in the other hadith, "His veil is light," so this light, and Allah knows best, is the light mentioned in the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him: "I saw a light."

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp﴾, is a likeness of His light in the heart of His believing servant, as Ubayy ibn Ka'b and others said. The pronoun in "His light" has been disputed. It has been said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., the likeness of the light of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that its referent is "the believer," i.e., the likeness of the light of the believer.

(p-٤٥٢٨) The correct view is that the pronoun refers back to Allah, Exalted is He. The meaning is: the likeness of the light of Allah, glory be to Him, in the heart of His servant. The greatest of His servants in their share of this light is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This, together with what the mentioned pronoun's return encompasses—and it is the natural sense of the discourse—includes the three estimations, and it is more complete in wording and meaning. This light is attributed to Allah, Exalted is He, since He is the One who bestows it upon His servant and grants it to him. It is also attributed to the servant, since he is its locus and its receiver. Thus it is attributed both to the Agent and to the Receiver. This light has an agent and a receiver, a locus and a bearer, and a substance. The verse has included the mention of all these matters in detail. The agent, namely Allah Exalted, is the Bestower of lights, who guides whom He wills to His light. The receiver is the believing servant. The locus is his heart. The bearer is his resolve, his determination and his will. The substance is his speech and his deed. This marvelous simile contained in the verse includes secrets and meanings and a manifestation of the completeness of His blessing upon His believing servant, through what He has bestowed upon him of His light, which gladdens the eyes of its people and delights their hearts.

There are two methods for this simile among the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani). The first: the method of the compound simile (al-tashbih al-murakkab), which is closer in its derivation and safer from artificiality. It is that the whole sentence, in its entirety, is likened to the light of the believer, without addressing the detail of each part of the likened item and matching it with a part of the likeness. Most of the Qur'an's parables follow this method. Consider the description of the niche (mishkah), which is a recess cut through so as to gather the light most fully. In it is placed a lamp, and that lamp is inside a glass that resembles a brilliant star in its clarity and beauty. Its fuel is from the purest and most complete of oils in fuel, from the oil of a tree in the midst of an orchard, neither eastern nor western, such that the sun does not strike it at one of the two ends of the day; rather it is in the midst of the orchard, protected by its edges, the sun striking it in the most balanced manner, and blights keep away from its edges. Because of the intensity of the brightness of its oil, its clarity and its beauty, it nearly gives light without fire touching it. This whole compound is the likeness of the light of Allah, Exalted, which He placed in the heart of His believing servant and specially granted to him.

The second method is the method of the detailed simile (al-tashbih al-mufassal). It has been said: the niche is the chest of the believer, and the glass is his heart. His heart is likened to glass for its delicacy, its clarity and its firmness. Likewise the heart of the believer, for it has combined the three attributes: he shows mercy, does good, is tender and compassionate toward creation through his delicacy and clarity. The forms of realities and knowledge are manifested in it as they truly are. Turbidity, filth and dirt recede in proportion to its clarity. By its firmness he is steadfast in the command of Allah Exalted, stands firm for the sake of Allah Exalted, and is stern toward the enemies of Allah Exalted. He upholds the truth for Allah Exalted. Allah Exalted has made hearts like vessels, as some of the early generations (al-salaf) said: "The hearts are the vessels of Allah in His earth, so the most beloved of them to Him are the most delicate, the firmest and the purest." The lamp is the light of faith in his heart. The blessed tree is the tree of revelation, which contains guidance and the religion of truth; it is the substance of the lamp from which it is kindled. "Light upon light" is the light of sound nature (al-fitrah al-sahihah), sound perception, and the light of revelation and the Book. So one light is added to the other, and the servant increases in light upon light. For this reason he nearly speaks the truth and wisdom before he hears what is in it by transmitted report (bi'l-athar). Then the transmitted report reaches him in the same way as what has occurred in his heart and what he has spoken. Thus the witness of reason, the Law, nature and revelation agree for him. His intellect, his nature and his taste show him that what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought is the truth, and reason and transmitted text never conflict for him at all; rather they confirm and agree with each other. This is the sign of light upon light. End. And the statement of Allah, Exalted:

**The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words:**

[36–38] ﴿In houses which God has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein He is glorified morning and evening, by men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of God, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat (obligatory alms). They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about, that God may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty; and God provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ [al-Nur: 37–38]

﴿In houses which God has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned﴾: that is, He commanded that they be held in honour, free from idle talk, or that they be raised in rank through construction. His name is recited in them, and no one other than Him is worshipped in them, because they were built upon His name, may His majesty be exalted. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is a qualifier (ṣifah) of (miṣbāh) or (zujājah), or it is related to (tūqadu), or to an implied verb; that is: "Glorify Him in houses." Or it is related to (yusabbiḥu). The word (fīhā) is a repetition for emphasis.

Abu al-Su'ud said: When He mentioned the matter of the Noble Qur'an in its explanation of the laws and rulings, their principles and their ultimate purposes, which entail reward and punishment, and it was indicated that it is in the utmost degree of clarification, being exemplified by the light of the niche (mishkah), He followed this with mention of the two groups and a depiction of some of their deeds that reveal the condition of their states concerning transgression and its absence. By "houses" is meant all the mosques. ﴿Therein He is glorified morning﴾: that is, before the rising of the sun. ﴿And evening﴾: the plural of aṣīl, which is the late afternoon before the setting of the sun. ﴿By men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Nur: 37]: that is, from glorifying and praising Him. ﴿And the establishment of prayer﴾ [al-Nur: 37]: that is, performing it at its appointed times without delay. ﴿And the giving of zakat﴾ [al-Nur: 37]: that is, the wealth by which its giver purifies himself from the defilement of stinginess and the vileness of miserliness, and his soul is cleansed and his inner self is made pure. ﴿They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾ [al-Nur: 37]: that is, they will be agitated and changed from terror and dread, as in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. ﴿That God may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty; and God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [al-Nur: 38]. The particle (li) (in order that) is related to (yusabbiḥu), or to (lā tulhīhim), or to an implied element indicated by the context; that is: they do what they do of what has been mentioned, in order that He may reward them. At the end of the verse there is an affirmation and an alert to the perfection of power, the effectiveness of will, and the vastness of benevolence, because (bi-ghayri ḥisāb, "without reckoning") is a metonymy for abundance. The meaning is that it does not fall under the reckoning and counting of creatures.

**Note:**

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): In this verse there is a command to honour the mosques and to keep them free from idle talk and filth. In it is also the recommendation of the remembrance of God and of prayer in the mosques. In His words, ﴿men﴾ [al-Nur: 37], there is an indication that the better course for women is to pray in the innermost part of their houses, as the hadith has stated explicitly, except on occasions such as the two festivals, due to the hadith: "Let them attend the good and the supplication of the Muslims." His words, ﴿whom neither trade distracts﴾ [al-Nur: 37], and the verse, indicate that trade does not contradict prayer, because the intent of the verse is that they engage in it, yet it does not distract them from prayer and from attending congregation. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Umar that he was in the market when the prayer was called, so they closed their shops and entered the mosque. Ibn Umar said: "It was about you that this was revealed: ﴿men whom neither trade distracts﴾ [al-Nur: 37]..." And he related similarly from al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Salim, Ata', and Mutarrif. End of quotation. And His, may He be exalted, words:
